subject: English
passage:
The following text is adapted from Margaret Cavendish's 1666 nonfiction book Observations upon Experimental Philosophy.

If I judge right, 'tis the duty of a natural philosopher to set everything in its own light, and to convey observations of natural phenomena upon their legitimate verification, and no other: I mean thus, (for I would be as explicit as I can) that where an observation is confirmed to her with adequate testimony, she ought to give the world the special attestation of its proper witness, or else she is not just to the observation: and where it comes without such adequate testimony, she ought to say so; otherwise she is not just to her own integrity.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Natural philosophers rarely have access to all the information relevant to a particular phenomenon, so no single work of science should be taken as definitive.
choices.B: Natural philosophers should clearly indicate the extent to which each of their sources is trustworthy.
choices.C: The only observations that a natural philosopher should report are those who are widely viewed as reliable.
choices.D: Because natural philosophers cannot tell whose observations they should trust, they should avoid relying on secondhand reports of phenomena.

explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it captures the main idea of the passage. The text establishes a dual obligation for natural philosophers regarding source credibility. Cavendish argues that when an observation 'is confirmed to her with adequate testimony, she ought to give the world the special attestation of its proper witness,' and when it 'comes without such adequate testimony, she ought to say so.' These parallel statements illustrate one principle: philosophers should transparently communicate source reliability. Choice B synthesizes this as 'clearly indicate the extent to which each of their sources is trustworthy'—encompassing both providing attestation for verified observations and acknowledging when verification is absent.
